title: Recording setup; aging and writing things down; house memories
description: Interviewer Isabel Miller introduces the 1975 interview of Elsie Nelson in Moscow, Idaho, and the two arrange the room. Elsie reflects on growing old and wanting to record memories, then recalls showing her brother Carl and grandchildren around the old house, including his boyhood prank of punching a hole in the plaster wall.

title: Walking to school; winter sleigh rides; broken window panes
description: Elsie describes walking to school in Moscow, attending a country school for only three weeks, and her father collecting children by sleigh on bad days before the family had a telephone. She tells how her father repaired broken window panes, finally walking to town to carry one home himself, highlighting farm self-sufficiency.

title: Father's farming priorities; school route; grandparents' visits
description: Elsie explains that her father focused on farming and hired out house-painting and papering. She recalls walking the railroad tracks to school, stopping at her grandparents' house to have dusty shoes wiped, and wearing good clothes rather than jeans.

title: Family of ten; bread baking; school lunches; home-cured meat
description: Elsie describes her large family of seven brothers and two sisters, her mother's weekly baking of forty loaves, and her own task of rising at five to make breakfast and pack lunches. She details wrapping sandwiches in wax paper and newspaper, the home-cured and dried beef, and butchering before Christmas.

title: Mother's town upbringing; household chores; discipline and organization
description: Elsie discusses her mother's adjustment from town life to the farm and her own preference for housekeeping over cooking, with brothers assigned to help. She describes her mother as an unmatched organizer and explains the parents' mutual, unquestioned discipline in which her father rarely spanked.

title: Canning fruit; children's clothing; dressmakers and shopping
description: Elsie recalls canning hundreds of jars of fruit and vegetables and climbing cherry trees while the boys found excuses to help their father. She discusses the boys' overalls and yearly new suits, her own dresses made by her mother or dressmakers, and her mother's insistence on quality fabric from Moscow merchants like Williamson's.

title: High school graduation; university prep; early college courses
description: Elsie recounts graduating from high school in 1909 in a class of six girls and one boy, her brothers attending the university's preparatory department, and the principal persuading her to begin university work early. She reflects on teachers' influence and her own determination.

title: Father's immigration; Pasco homestead; move to Spokane Falls
description: Elsie tells of her father's birth on a Baltic island, his arrival in Philadelphia, mining in Colorado, and the failed homestead attempt near Pasco on the Columbia River, where an Indian woman ferried travelers on horseback. The men abandoned the desert claim and headed to Spokane Falls, where her father took a railroad contract.

title: Praise for young people; land use here and in Europe
description: Elsie praises the high school students who visit her and expresses faith in young people despite talk of bad ones. She complains about overcrowded cities and compares American land waste unfavorably with the intensive farming she observed in Scandinavia, Holland, and France.

title: Women in college; advice to a young couple; value of education
description: Elsie discusses how many women attended college in her day and recounts urging a former student to persuade his young wife to try college. She argues young people should set goals and save money, though she does not believe college is necessary for everyone.

title: Mother's reading while churning; magazines; Swedish heritage; church libraries
description: Elsie remembers her mother churning butter with a baby in one arm and a magazine in the other, and names the family's periodicals. She traces her parents' Swedish origins, her grandparents' life in Minnesota and Moscow, her own later study of Swedish, and the church libraries the family used.

title: Reading and inspiration
description: Elsie recounts how her mother cherished reading and her Sunday school teacher inspired her.

title: Mother and family dynamics
description: The discussion turns to Elsie's mother, her numerous children, and their lives on the farm.

title: Marriage and personal choices
description: Elsie shares her thoughts on marriage and why she chose not to settle down.

title: Health and care
description: Elsie describes her mother's health issues and her own experiences with medical care.

title: Views on women's roles
description: The interview explores Elsie's views on women's contributions and the feminist movement.

title: Writing and family history
description: She talks about her ambitions to document her family's history through writing.

title: Friendship and travel
description: Elsie discusses her friendships and travels, highlighting her passion for meeting new people.

title: Moscow Hotel dining room; Pullman customers; banquets and staff; feediing athletic teams
description: Elsie Nelson explains how she took the dining room job at the Moscow Hotel despite planning to move to California, endured a shabby room, and attracted Pullman faculty families until they filled the Sunday dining room and booked frequent banquets. She describes planning all special menus, struggling to find and supervise wartime help, and working five o'clock to nine or ten without rest to keep parties served correctly. She also details feeding visiting football and basketball teams from schools like Stanford, Oregon, and the University of Washington, ordering steak loins in advance, serving late-night sandwich and milkshake feeds, and befriending coaches and Portland Oregonian sportswriter L.H. Gregory, who wrote about her.

title: Daily restaurant and traveling salesmen; buying standards
description: Nelson moves on to the hotel's daily restaurant service, especially for traveling salesmen who timed their routes to eat there. She tells how she ordered from food salesmen but refused to be talked into pie fillings and convenience foods, insisting on fresh, home-style meals, which kept the traveling public coming back.
